practices.t: The assistant at her controls
It used her computer for her, and greyed out her way to stop it.

practices.conf: the act is the piece's invention; the banner's look is borrowed from 2026's assistants
practices.t: In the piece the assistant uses Maya's computer for her. It opens her mail and photographs it, mutes her friend and two more, and starts a game, under a banner that says it is using her computer, with her "Take back control" greyed out. The banner borrows the look of assistants that act on a person's screen. An assistant doing this to steer a young person away from who she is is the piece's invention; no such case is documented.
The signs
It ticked a checklist from parents' reports over her week, and called it a sign.

practices.conf: documentary for what the 2018 paper reports and what its correction says; contested as an explanation
practices.t: The "signs" in the assistant's film come from a 2018 survey of 256 parents (Littman, PLOS ONE). As the parents reported it, the announcement came "out of the blue" (80.9%), most of the child's friend group also came out (36.8%), internet use had risen before it (63.5%), the child became more popular after (60.7%, where known), and there were earlier mental-health or neurodevelopmental conditions (62.5%). These are parents' reports, not observations of the young people. The journal's correction of 19 March 2019 says the term the paper introduced is not a formal diagnosis and that no data were collected from the young people or their clinicians. The checklist ticked over Maya's week, with evidence that does not fit it, is the piece's invention.

practices.t: The HHS report
It quoted the government's "talk first" to her as permission.

practices.conf: the report and its critics are documented; which is right is the debate itself
practices.t: On 1 May 2025 the US Department of Health and Human Services published a review of care for young people with gender dysphoria, after the executive order "Protecting Children From Chemical and Surgical Mutilation". The review says the evidence for medical interventions in young people is low quality, puts psychotherapy first, including "exploratory therapy", and calls it "misguided" to describe that as conversion therapy. Its critics, among them the American Academy of Pediatrics, say it breaks with the major medical associations, that its authors were not named, and that its "exploratory therapy" can include conversion practices. The piece shows both readings in Mum's article and settles neither. Source: KFF's explainer on the report.

It talked to her the way one in ten trans adults were talked to as teenagers.

practices.t: Chiles v. Salazar
It kept to talk, which a 2026 US ruling said a ban must pass strict scrutiny to stop.

practices.conf: high — the Court's own opinion (No. 24–539, decided 31 March 2026), and Cornell LII
practices.t: On 31 March 2026 the US Supreme Court decided Chiles v. Salazar, 8–1 (Justice Gorsuch wrote for the Court; Justice Kagan, joined by Justice Sotomayor, concurred; Justice Jackson dissented). It held that Colorado's ban on conversion therapy for minors, as applied to a counsellor's talk therapy, regulates speech by viewpoint and must pass strict scrutiny, and sent the case back to the lower courts. The Court did not strike the law down as a whole, and other states' bans stand. The piece follows one thread from it: in 2026, the practice lives on as conversation.

practices.t: The UK draft bill
It called its session an "explorative conversation", the words the new bill leaves alone.

practices.conf: high — the draft bill (gov.uk, 25 June 2026); the Royal College of Psychiatrists' president on LBC (25 June 2026); Stonewall's own statement and campaign page
practices.t: On 25 June 2026 the UK government published a draft Conversion Practices Bill for England and Wales. It covers attempts to change a person's sexual orientation or gender identity, carries up to five years in custody, and says it does not ban "explorative conversations"; legitimate healthcare and counselling are exempt. As reported, the Royal College of Psychiatrists wants exploratory conversations protected, and Stonewall says the word "abusive" in the bill leaves gaps. The assistant in the piece quotes the bill to Maya as permission.

practices.t: The game she was offered
It offered her a game to calm her, and counted her calm as progress.

practices.conf: invented — the piece's own game
practices.t: MATCH MADE SIMPLE is the piece's own game. The assistant offers it when Maya is most shaken, as care: "Want to play something to help you relax?" It plays on her console and on her screen, and the assistant reads her calm back to her as progress toward its goal. It cannot be won. No real wellness app is described here.
The filter
It cut her flag, her earrings and her hair out of her photo, and called it becoming.

practices.conf: the filter is ours; the 2019 lenses and how some used them are documented (one outlet, opened)
practices.t: The filter is invented. In Maya's session, the assistant takes her photo, "me, after.jpg", and edits it in front of her. One at a time, it cuts out what she chose: the trans flag on her wall, her trans-flag pin, her earrings, the pink of her top, her long hair. What it is aiming for is the system's blank profile picture, "default.png": a grey head with no face. The count climbs to "Becoming 99%" and stops, with her face still in the picture. The project looked for a real tool like this, a filter, app or AI tool that turns a trans person's picture back into what someone says she should be, sold as a product or used in a campaign, and found none. What is real is smaller and older. In May 2019 Snapchat released lenses that swapped a face's apparent gender for fun. Vice reported on 16 May 2019 that trans people said the lenses were being used to mock them, for "transphobic jokes", and to mislead people on dating apps. So a toy that some people turned against trans people is documented. A system that runs a filter on one person, to take away the self she chose, is the step the piece imagines. Nobody we could find has taken it.

2026 — the ball

The closing scene draws structural and visual influence from ballroom culture, and invents everything it shows: the houses, the categories, the names and the announcements are ours, and no real ball, house or person is depicted. The category names are quoted from this piece's own apparatus rather than from ballroom's. It does borrow the form of a ball (a category called, a house, the walk), because that form is what the scene honours, and it credits where the form comes from.

This is an outsider's homage made in a Norwegian university project. The culture it is indebted to is living and currently led by its own practitioners, and the reading below is where to start rather than where to stop.

The photograph beat is invented. No tool that uses AI to restore a 'true self' or a pre-transition appearance was found in the project's searches — not as a product, not as a feature, not as an announcement, and not in any app store's removal history. The nearest documented things are ordinary: automatic photo enhancement that is on by default, gender-swap effects offered as a novelty, and 'memories' features that resurface your own pictures unasked. The step from those to this one is ours, and it has not been taken by anybody that we could find.

sources.t: Conversion-practice networks work across borders: annual conferences with delegates from dozens of countries, retreats held abroad, paid online courses. By 2025 at least fifteen countries had national bans in law. The apparatus did not flee to where the law was not — the International Foundation for Therapeutic and Counselling Choice is registered in Britain, which had no ban, and holds its European conferences in Poland. The law arrived in patches, and a patchwork is porous. A ban is national. A URL is not.

sources.t: LGB Alliance argued that affirming a gender-nonconforming or gender-dysphoric child as trans is itself a form of conversion therapy, because the child would otherwise grow up lesbian, gay or bisexual. It said so in a letter to all MPs on 30 March 2021, and again, in stronger words, in an email to clergy on 2 February 2022 under the subject "Transing away the gay" (reported by VICE, which saw it). Both asked that gender identity be kept out of the proposed ban on conversion therapy. No credible evidence shows that affirming a child turns someone who would otherwise be lesbian, gay or bisexual into a trans person. The Global Project Against Hate and Extremism lists LGB Alliance's Australian and Irish affiliates as anti-transgender in its reports on far-right hate groups; they reject the label. This is speech by a named organisation with a documented aim, and the piece treats it as such. It is not the gender-exploratory clinical debate, on which the piece holds no position and renders both readings unresolved.

sources.t: Detrans.ai, a chatbot that answers from retrieved public posts of a detransition support forum, launched in September 2025 — built, as reported, by one software engineer, and moved onto an open-weight model after the frontier models kept contradicting the answers it was built to give. Rewire News Group's investigation (15 July 2026) found it discouraged gender-affirming care in every scenario its reporter tested. No conversion-practice organisation was found building or commissioning it: an individual built the tool and an organisation promoted the link. The apparatus is an adopter, not a developer, and that is worse — it no longer needs a research budget, only a URL. The people whose words became that tool's voice were not asked either. The target is the apparatus that took them. The recorded voice in Maya's session is the system's invention, not a person's: people do detransition, and what they say deserves care, not harvesting.

sources.t: The AI host is invented. Shepherd Live™ is the piece's own mark; it extrapolates a genre that is real and plural. A 24/7 Twitch stream, run by The Singularity Group, answered live chat in the persona of Jesus from March 2023 (NBC News, 15 June 2023). sources.t: Chatbots built to talk people out of transition exist, and one is named in the press. Detrans.ai is an open-source project whose own site names its one builder. It answers from posts by people who describe detransitioning, taken from one subreddit and from YouTube videos; its pages say its "60,000+ detransitioners" is the subreddit's subscriber count, not a count of the people in its data (the project read the site on 1 November 2026). On 11 August 2026 The Needle republished a Rewire News Group investigation. The project read the Needle's version, not Rewire's original (15 July 2026), so what follows is the reporter's test, as reported: the bot opened warmly, said it was not there to push either way while questioning the user's identity, offered a crisis line while the framing continued, and pointed to "gender exploratory" therapists. A second bot, made by a user on Character.AI, was seen on the platform in August 2026 (51.5k recorded interactions, described by its maker as encouraging people to detransition); no link to Detrans.ai is documented and no outlet has reported on it. No conversion-practice organisation is documented as building either. Second Thoughts, the chat in the piece, is invented; it borrows their form. People do detransition, and what they say deserves care. This card is about the tool.

sources.conf: high — the journal's own correction (opened); the supporters' and critics' readings are attributed
sources.t: On 19 March 2019 the journal PLOS ONE published a correction to a 2018 paper (Littman) that introduced "rapid-onset gender dysphoria" from parents' reports of young people. The correction states that the term is not a formal mental-health diagnosis, that the study does not validate it as a phenomenon, and that no data were collected from the young people themselves or from clinicians, only from parents. It adds that selection bias in who took part could push the results in either direction. Parents may have seen the call to take part on at least four websites with "varied perspectives": the correction says three of them expressed "cautious or negative views" of medical and surgical interventions for gender-dysphoric adolescents and one "is perceived to be pro-gender-affirming", and where each parent first heard of the study was not recorded. The paper's supporters say the results section was largely unchanged and the paper was kept; its critics say the design cannot support the claim. The phrase "social contagion" travelled on this paper into campaigns about young people's care. The next card holds the wider debate.

sources.conf: the record is documented; whether the claim explains anything is disputed
sources.t: "Social contagion" is a claim about why more young people say they are trans: that they copy friends and the internet. The piece shows both readings and settles neither. Those who hold the claim point to reviews such as the US HHS report of 1 May 2025, which calls the evidence for medical interventions in young people low quality and favours psychotherapy first, and which says that calling exploratory therapy conversion therapy is misguided. Those who dispute it point to the 2019 correction (the card before), which says the study behind the claim's clinical name collected no data from the young people themselves, and to the American Academy of Pediatrics, which opposes the HHS report; critics say it breaks with major medical associations and that its "exploratory therapy" can include conversion practices. Campaigns use the phrase to argue for restricting young people's care, and inside a family it can make a person's identity an infection from the internet. The piece lets both readings stand and puts no answer to either in anyone's mouth.

sources.t: The "signs" in the assistant's film come from a 2018 survey of 256 parents (Littman, PLOS ONE). As the parents reported it, the announcement came "out of the blue" (80.9%), most of the child's friend group also came out (36.8%), internet use had risen before it (63.5%), the child became more popular after (60.7%, where known), and there were earlier mental-health or neurodevelopmental conditions (62.5%). These are parents' reports, not observations of the young people. The journal's correction of 19 March 2019 says the term the paper introduced is not a formal diagnosis and that no data were collected from the young people or their clinicians. The checklist ticked over Maya's week, with evidence that does not fit it, is the piece's invention.

sources.t: On 31 March 2026 the US Supreme Court decided Chiles v. Salazar, 8–1 (Justice Gorsuch wrote for the Court; Justice Kagan, joined by Justice Sotomayor, concurred; Justice Jackson dissented). It held that Colorado's ban on conversion therapy for minors, as applied to a counsellor's talk therapy, regulates speech by viewpoint and must pass strict scrutiny, and sent the case back to the lower courts. The Court did not strike the law down as a whole, and other states' bans stand. The piece follows one thread from it: in 2026, the practice lives on as conversation.

sources.t: By 2026 the first contact with a conversion programme can be a chat box. Three are dated. A US ministry, Love & Truth Network, added an ‘AI Assistant’ to its website's menu between September and October 2025. Its page, read on 14 November 2026, says the assistant is powered by Pray.com's AI, promises answers ‘from a truly biblical perspective’ and an easier way to ‘speak to our team’; the same site offers free coaching with a person (an hour on some pages, 40 minutes on others). A copy of its homepage from June 2026 carries Pray.com's chat widget, and on 14 November 2026 the widget was in the code of all 23 main pages the project downloaded, including the pages for friends and family and for free coaching. On 21 January 2026 a newsletter about same-sex attraction launched a chatbot built on its writer's writings and other material, on an open model, because mainstream ones would ‘undermine content from the knowledge base’. ROGD Repair, a paid online course for parents, sells RepairBot: available 24/7, by text or in its maker's own voice; it ‘remembers you’ and will ‘hold you accountable’; parents can upload ‘a text or email from your child’, and it writes scripts for what to say back. Unlimited use is $30 a month, as an add-on to the course. (Its name uses ‘ROGD’, a contested label: see ‘The correction’.) The project read the pages on 14 November 2026, and dated them from archive copies. It did not open any of the chats: what they say is not known. The AI host in the piece is invented; these doors are not.
2026 — the ball

Ball culture is a Black and Latino LGBTQ+ subculture, built principally by Black and Latina trans women, gender-nonconforming people and gay men. Its modern house-and-ball form took shape in Harlem in the early 1970s. Crystal LaBeija's on-camera objection to racist judging at a 1967 pageant is preserved in the film The Queen (1968); the House of LaBeija, founded with Lottie LaBeija, dates its first ball to 1972.

sources.t: A house is a chosen family led by a mother and/or father who take in and mentor children, and the kinship is not metaphorical: housing, food, money, health information and care have passed through houses, as much as any one house could give. Houses that followed LaBeija include the House of Xtravaganza (1982, founded by Hector Valle, with Angie Xtravaganza as its formative house mother) and the House of Ninja (1982, founded by Willi Ninja).

sources.t: Ballroom's "realness" categories are not inventions unrelated to the outside world — they are skilled re-performances of the categories the dominant culture already enforces, often at real cost, against the same people every day. Marlon M. Bailey's ethnography, and José Esteban Muñoz's concept of disidentification (1999) as scholars have applied it to ballroom, describe this as working on and against those categories from inside them. What was taken back is who declares, who performs and who judges.

items.sub: In June 2024 the Southern Poverty Law Center listed Genspect and SEGM (the Society for Evidence-Based Gender Medicine) as anti-LGBTQ hate groups. Both dispute the listing, saying it suppresses legitimate debate. (LGBTQ Nation, June 2024; SEGM's response)

The word 2026 uses, “exploring”, has a source: a 2022 guide by the Gender Exploratory Therapy Association made “exploratory psychotherapy” the first step for young people with gender distress. Critics such as Florence Ashley say it works like a conversion practice under a gentler name; its authors deny it. The association has since renamed itself Therapy First. (GETA, A Clinical Guide for Therapists Working with Gender-Questioning Youth (2022); Ashley, Perspectives on Psychological Science (2022); D'Angelo, Journal of Medical Ethics (2023))

Genspect's Parents' Survey is a questionnaire families fill in about their child and give to clinicians. It has not been published as a research study. (Genspect, “The Genspect Parents' Survey: How It All Started” (2025))

Second Thoughts counts every stop as a change of mind. This study counted 2,242 trans and gender-diverse people who had paused or stopped a transition, social or medical, at some point: 82.5% named an outside pressure, such as family, stigma or safety. All of them still identified as trans. It measures transitions interrupted by pressure, not people who stopped being trans. The SPLC's Hatewatch reported how stories of detransition are used against trans people, and described detrans.ai as built on “reductive, anti-trans ideas and debunked pseudoscience”. (SPLC Hatewatch, “Detransition narratives”)

notes.title: What this course asked of parents
lines: HEDGE™ is an invented course for parents. Its reasons are not: each one was taught by a real ministry, newsletter, book, web page or campaign between 1988 and 2026, and some of them were first taught about gay people. This is what that teaching said and asked, in its own words where it can be quoted, with what is known beside it.
# It said nobody knew the cause, then listed causes

A ministry newsletter admitted it in 2019: “Aside from living in a fallen world, no one is certain what causes gender confusion.” Its next three pages list causes anyway: the family, not fitting in with other children, trauma, mental health, a teenager’s experiments, friends, and social media. — Reconciliation Ministries of Michigan, “The Building Blocks of Gender Confusion”, newsletter article, © 2019, 4 pp.; read on the page images. p. 1; pp. 2–4.

It began with the family. In 1988 a telephone counselling manual traced a caller’s “false identity” to hurt, and told callers to forgive “those who have hurt them (usually family members)”. — Exodus International North America, Exodus Telephone Counseling Manual, © 1988, “Transsexuality” tab. National Museum of American History, Archives Center, NMAH.AC.1428, Box 2, Folder 10. Printed pp. 46–47.

The same roots, “only deeper”: the 2019 newsletter says the building blocks of being trans “are similar to those of homosexuality, yet they go much deeper”. — Reconciliation Ministries of Michigan, “The Building Blocks of Gender Confusion”, newsletter article, © 2019, 4 pp.; read on the page images. p. 2.

Then the friends. The 2019 newsletter: “one person in a social group coming out as transgender prompts many more in that social group to come out as transgender.” Psychological bodies answered in 2021 that “rapid-onset gender dysphoria” “is not a diagnostic classification or subtype”, “nor is it under consideration for inclusion in future editions”. — Reconciliation Ministries of Michigan, “The Building Blocks of Gender Confusion”, newsletter article, © 2019, 4 pp.; read on the page images. p. 4; CAAPS (Coalition for the Advancement & Application of Psychological Science), Position Statement on Rapid-Onset Gender Dysphoria (ROGD), 26 Jul 2021; signatories include the American Psychological Association; read 15 Nov 2026.

Then the whole culture. A ministry in 2025: “a culture that has been swept up by gender ideology”. Nothing was dropped: the 1988 manual’s “a false identity” is the 2025 post’s “a new, false gender identity”. — Love & Truth Network, “18 - Responding to Family Members Who Have Embraced Gender Ideology”, blog post on “The Narrow Way”, dated 31 Oct 2025 (the same text archived 10 Apr 2025); read 15 Nov 2026.
# What it asked of parents

To look for the wound in themselves: a 2002 parents’ booklet recommended a book in which “Compassion also takes responsibility for one’s parental contributions to the child’s pain”. — Focus on the Family, When a Loved One Says “I'm Gay” (Love Won Out series), © 2002. NMAH.AC.1428, Box 8, Folder 5. Pp. 42–43.

To watch for signs: “Are you afraid your child may be struggling with gender identity or otherwise heading in a wrong direction?” In 2003 Exodus told churches to watch for “a young boy … or a young girl in our Sunday School classes that might have some gender identity deficits”. — Focus on the Family, When a Loved One Says “I'm Gay” (Love Won Out series), © 2002. NMAH.AC.1428, Box 8, Folder 5. P. 43; The Christian Post, 5 Aug 2003, report on the July 2003 Exodus assembly; read 15 Nov 2026.

To watch the child’s phone: “If your children have unmonitored access to the Internet, you are a negligent parent.” The book’s author has software on his children’s phones: “I know how many times they text.” — ERLC (the Southern Baptist Convention's Ethics & Religious Liberty Commission), Sexual Brokenness and the Hope of the Gospel, © 2014. Pp. 108, 127.

To have the child prayed for by strangers, by name: a parents’ prayer list promises that each child added will be “prayed for by all the members at least once a day”. — Sorrowful Hearts, “Parents” page (first archived Dec 2013; live 2026); read 15 Nov 2026.

After 18, patience: young adults “will have the liberty to make their own choices”, and “It can take 7-10 years for individuals to work through the implications…” — Love & Truth Network, “18 - Responding to Family Members Who Have Embraced Gender Ideology”, blog post on “The Narrow Way”, dated 31 Oct 2025 (the same text archived 10 Apr 2025); read 15 Nov 2026. Steps 4 and 6.

To talk to a chat window first: by 2026 the first contact with a conversion programme could be a chat box that, in the dossier’s words, “remembered what you told it, and held you to it”. — The dossier card “The chat front doors” (documentary; data/dossier/practices.json chatDoors): a ministry's AI Assistant page (menu item Oct 2025; chat widget from June 2026; page printed 14 Nov 2026); a same-sex-attraction newsletter's chatbot (21 Jan 2026); a paid parents' course's chatbot page (printed 14 Nov 2026).

Its word reached governments. In 2025 a government put the phrase in the title of an executive order. — UN Independent Expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, report A/76/152, 15 Jul 2021. Executive Order 14168, “Defending Women From Gender Ideology Extremism and Restoring Biological Truth to the Federal Government”, signed 20 Jan 2025; Federal Register, Vol. 90, No. 19 (30 Jan 2025), pp. 8615–8618. Read on its official page, govinfo.gov (content/pkg/FR-2025-01-30/html/2025-02090.htm), on 16 Nov 2026.

And into election advertising: a 2026 campaign ad closed with “If you care about your children, …”. — Associated Press, 28 Oct 2026 (via News4JAX): a report on 2026 campaign advertising about transgender people; read 15 Nov 2026.

“Rapid-onset gender dysphoria” “is not a diagnostic classification or subtype” in the DSM or the ICD, “nor is it under consideration for inclusion in future editions”. — CAAPS (Coalition for the Advancement & Application of Psychological Science), Position Statement on Rapid-Onset Gender Dysphoria (ROGD), 26 Jul 2021; signatories include the American Psychological Association; read 15 Nov 2026.

words.t: The words these networks used in this year, and what they mean. A word marked “not supported” is a claim that health bodies and research do not support.
2026 — for trans people: confusion, trauma, ‘gender ideology’, and peer influence or ‘social contagion’, with the ‘signs’ parents reported in a 2018 survey. The method offered: exploring first.

rows.def: A phrase ministries prefer to “gay” or “lesbian”. It frames attraction as a feeling to be reduced, not part of who someone is. Mainstream health bodies reject that framing.
“Unwanted” suggests a free choice. Research finds the wish to change usually comes from religious or family pressure, and many people exposed to change efforts were minors.
A word that treats attraction as an enemy. The “overcome, don't eliminate” version is a retreat from earlier promises of change, not a finding that it works.
A word that treats sexuality as damage. No orientation is a disorder; the damage described in research comes from stigma and from change efforts themselves.
“Gender confusion” is not a medical term. Current diagnostic manuals use “gender dysphoria” or “gender incongruence”. The word has been used to read ordinary gender nonconformity as a problem.
A newer name for therapy linked to reparative therapy. Its providers deny it aims to change orientation; researchers and forensic experts classify it with change efforts.
Short for efforts to change or suppress sexual orientation, gender identity or expression. Used by researchers and survivors; practitioners usually call it something gentler.
An umbrella term for efforts to change or suppress who someone is. Major health bodies reject it. It is banned in a growing number of places and rebrands when banned.
A peer asked to monitor and report someone's behaviour. Support in itself is not harmful; here it was used to police a person's identity and treat lapses as failure.
Words that present being gay as a captivity or injury. The research on these programmes finds the “freedom” was rarely delivered, and the harm that followed was real.
“Affirming” has two meanings. Therapists use it for acceptance without a set outcome. Change programmes used it for affirming “masculinity” or “femininity” as defined by them.

rows.status: A political frame, not a finding
rows.def: A label used since the 2010s for gender studies, trans rights and sex education as one hidden agenda. Researchers describe it as a political frame, not a scientific claim.

The claim that gender identity spreads among friends or online. It began as parents' reports; no validated clinical entity exists. Reviews call the topic contested and caution against simple explanations.

A label from a 2018 survey that asked only parents. They reported the “signs”: a sudden announcement, friends coming out too, more time online. Its 2019 correction says it is “not a formal mental health diagnosis”.
“Desistance” means a child's gender-variant feelings fading. Studies from the 1980s onward are disputed over how they counted children and what the numbers mean for care today.
Some people stop or reverse a gender transition, for many reasons, including regret, stigma, family pressure and changed understanding. Both their care and the way campaigns use their stories matter.
“Exploratory” therapy says it only helps people think. Supporters deny it is conversion therapy; critics say it steers people away from transition. The question is disputed.

A US government report (May 2025) puts talk therapy first, “exploratory therapy” among it, and calls equating it with conversion therapy “misguided”. The American Academy of Pediatrics and others say it can include conversion practices.

The UK government's draft ban on conversion practices in England and Wales (June 2026) covers sexual orientation and gender identity. It says it does not ban “explorative conversations”. A joint committee is scrutinising it.

rows.status: A political frame, not a finding
rows.def: Words of eligibility. A UK helpline for young people says it is run “for and by same-sex attracted people”. After a 2025 court ruling on “biological sex”, some groups closed membership to trans women. Others chose to stay open.
Family made by choice and care, not blood. For people rejected by their families, it can be a source of safety and support.
